captions.instagram:
How do floods happen?

A flood is water arriving faster than it can leave. Pour rain on a 3D valley, see how forest, farmland and paving split it between soaking in and running off, drive a river's hydrograph over its banks, and work out live why a "100-year flood" has a one in four chance of reaching you in 30 years.

→ A river carries the rain of its whole catchment: every slope and stream that drains to it.
→ When rain runs off faster than the channel can carry it, the river takes back its floodplain.
→ A forest soaks up most of a storm. Paving sends nearly all of it straight to the drains.
→ After a storm the river rises to a peak, hours later, and then falls. That curve is its hydrograph.
→ Pave the catchment and straighten the channels, and the same rain gives a higher, earlier peak.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/floodclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.description:
A flood is water arriving faster than it can leave. Pour rain on a 3D valley, see how forest, farmland and paving split it between soaking in and running off, drive a river's hydrograph over its banks, and work out live why a "100-year flood" has a one in four chance of reaching you in 30 years.

In this video:
• A river and its valley. A catchment is all the land that slopes to one river.
• Where the rain goes. Rain in equals water caught, water soaked in and runoff.
• The river's pulse. After a storm a river rises to a peak and falls: its hydrograph.
• Six kinds of flood. River floods rise over days.
• Odds and defences. A 100-year flood has a 1 % chance each year, which adds up to about 26 % over 30 years.
• India and staying safe. India gets most of its rain in four monsoon months.
